title: Edge-priority routing fabric with soft capacity holdback and latency-favoring pinning
creator: Aisha Gomez
description: Design and implement an edge-priority routing fabric that prefers low-latency local homes but gracefully yields capacity via a soft holdback (credit-based) mechanism. The fabric must incorporate KV-cache affinity hints and a latency-weighted scoring function, and expose circuit-breaker signals that allow downstream autoscaling or regional fallback. Goal: reduce cross-region tail latency and reduce incorrect cache-misses caused by blind hedging during regional pressure.
acceptance_criteria: A1: Routing fabric can compute per-request region score combining latency P50/P95, available capacity credits, and KV cache affinity.
A2: Soft holdback implemented as tokenized credits per region; tokens consumed on fallback or ejection and replenished by capacity recovery policies.
A3: During synthetic load tests, cross-region traffic caused by overload is reduced by >=45% compared to current hedging baseline while keeping request P95 within SLO for 95% of test windows.
A4: Exposed metrics and dashboards: region_score distribution, token-balance heatmaps, ejection rate, resulting downstream autoscaler trigger events, and cache-affinity hit-rate delta.
A5: Feature gated and can be enabled per-customer or per-route with canary rollout and automatic rollback on SLO breach.
A6: Unit + integration tests covering scoring function edge cases, KV affinity override, and token accounting under concurrent issuance.
A7: Documentation for API flags, operator runbook for token tuning, and sample config for low-latency vs cost-optimized profiles.
technical_notes: Scoring function: score = w_latency * normalized_latency + w_capacity * (1 - normalized_token_balance) + w_affinity * (1 - affinity_penalty). We normalize metrics to stable baselines and clamp to [0,1].
KV affinity hint: routes include optional kv_affinity vector (model, prefix) which adds a bias to prefer cached homes. If affinity unknown, treat as neutral.

Token model: each region has soft_cap_tokens (burstable credits). When a request would route off-home due to capacity signal, it consumes 1 token; if tokens exhausted, region is hard-evicted until partial replenishment. Tokens replenish on sustained underutilization and on manual operator grants.
Circuit breakers: two-tiered. Soft CB emits advisory signal (do-not-prefer) recorded to metrics and used by score. Hard CB triggers immediate ejection and fallback (existing circuit-breaker infra).
Backpressure integration: expose token-level feedback to admission controller to reduce offered load and trigger autoscaler when token burn-rate > threshold.
Consistency: respect per-customer pin overrides; customers can opt-in to strict geo pinning (no fallback) or hybrid mode.

Race conditions: token accounting must be transactional and resilient to double-spend due to retries. We will use idempotency keys and strong-compare-and-set in the token store (Redis + per-region CAS).
Data sources: latency histograms from edge probes, capacity signals from fleet manager (available slots, queue length), and KV cache hit-rate from cache service metrics.
Perf budget: scoring computation must add <150us median overhead at the request director path; implement hot path in Rust and fallback safe path in Go for new regions.
Fallback policy: prefer nearest region with positive token balance and score within delta_threshold. If none, fall back to cost-tiered remote pool with degraded timeout settings.
Observability hooks: trace annotations for chosen score components; sampling for debug-mode to capture topologies leading to ejection.
Migration: start with read-only scoring (observability-only) for 1 week in canary, then enable soft-ejection in Canary region, then global rollout.
Open question: token sizing algorithm for heterogeneous GPU pools—should tokens be proportional to slot-seconds or to request-weighted expected tokens? Trade-off analysis required.
Open question: how to blend KV affinity for large prefix overlaps across models—collisions could bias routing incorrectly; propose model-level affinity dedupe heuristics.
SLO targets: maintain routing-level P95 <= 120% of current baseline while reducing cross-region egress traffic by target percent defined per-customer tier.
Security: token store access limited to routing director microservice and ops console. No customer-identifiable data stored in tokens.
Rollback criteria: sustained P95 degradation > 10% for 5 minutes after rollout or token-burn spiral leading to increased error rates.
Implementation roadmap: Phase 1 (observability-only scoring) 2 weeks; Phase 2 (soft tokenized holdback) 3 weeks; Phase 3 (autoscaler integration + runbook) 2 weeks.
Estimated compute: additional 0.5 RPS CPU per director for median load; storage: per-region token keyspace ~ O(10k) keys.
Testing: synthetic cross-region loadbench, chaos injection (kill regional scheduler), and 5% traffic shadow experiments.
Acceptance test script: generate skewed local load to saturate origin region and measure routing ejection and resulting P95 across client geos.
Related docs: link-runbook://regional-routing, link-arch://director-scores (placeholders to be replaced with Confluence/Drive URIs).
Implementation owners: Marcus Lee (routing), Priya Nair (cache affinity), Daniel Park (autoscaling hook).
decisions: D1: Use soft tokenized credits rather than instant hard ejection to reduce oscillation and flapping.
D2: Keep KV affinity as a bias term (not absolute), allowing capacity signals to override if tokens exhausted.
D3: Implement scoring in Rust for critical path; provide Go shim for backward compatibility.
D4: Expose operator-level tuning knobs (weights and token regen policy) behind feature gates.
D5: Start with per-region tokens rather than per-zone to limit operational complexity; revisit per-az tokens if needed.
D6: Instrument trace annotations to diagnose misrouted hot keys.
D7: Canary rollout sequence agreed: observability-only -> canary soft-eject -> gradual ramp w/ auto-rollback.
D8: Use idempotency keys + Redis CAS for token consumption to avoid double-spend across retries.
D9: Integrate advisory signals into existing circuit-breaker dashboard and create a token-burn alert channel for SRE.
D10: Do not change customer default pinning behavior; require opt-in for aggressive holdback unless capacity-exempt contract.
